name: Robert Citron

summary.text: Robert L. Citron was Treasurer-Tax Collector of Orange County, California, and ran the county investment pool whose losses led the county to file for bankruptcy on December 6, 1994. On April 27, 1995 he pleaded guilty in Orange County Superior Court to six felony counts; in November 1996 he was sentenced to a year in jail and a $100,000 fine. The SEC sued him in January 1996 and he consented to a permanent injunction. The county's suit against Merrill Lynch, its principal broker, was settled in 1998 for $400 million without admission of wrongdoing.

sources.title: The 4/95 Plea/Sentencing Agreement Of Bob Citron Re: His Criminal Role In The Orange County Bankruptcy

facts.claim: On April 27, 1995 Citron signed a plea agreement under which he would be arraigned that day and plead guilty to all charges and admit all enhancements; the six felony counts comprised two counts of untrue material statements in the sale of securities under the California Corporations Code and four Penal Code counts covering misappropriation of public funds, failure to transfer public funds and false entries in a public record.
facts.quote: plead guilty to all charges and admit all enhancements

sources.title: The 4/95 Plea/Sentencing Agreement Of Bob Citron

facts.claim: The Los Angeles Times reported that Citron entered his plea before Judge David O. Carter in Orange County Superior Court, that he faced up to 14 years in prison, that the misappropriation counts involved county investment losses shifted to other pool participants, and that prosecutors found no evidence of personal gain by Citron.
facts.quote: The Times account says the misappropriation counts involved county investment losses that were shifted to other pool participants, and that prosecutors found no evidence of personal gain by Citron.

facts.claim: In November 1996 Citron was sentenced to a year in jail and a $100,000 fine.
facts.quote: Robert Citron, the person at the center of the Orange County billion-dollar bankruptcy, was sentenced to a year in jail and a $100,000 fine.

sources.title: Elaine Korry reports: Robert Citron, the person at the center...

sources.publisher: Philippe Jorion, UC Irvine (case study mirrored by University of Trier)
sources.title: Orange County case

facts.claim: On January 24, 1996 the SEC filed a complaint against Citron and former assistant treasurer Matthew Raabe alleging misstatements and omissions in official statements for more than $2.1 billion of municipal securities issued in 1993 and 1994; on May 9, 1996 the court entered final judgments permanently enjoining both men from future antifraud violations, to which they consented without admitting or denying the allegations.
facts.quote: Citron and Raabe consented to permanent injunctions against future antifraud violations without admitting or denying the allegations

facts.claim: In June 1998 Merrill Lynch, Orange County's chief investment banker at the time of the bankruptcy, agreed to pay the county $400 million to settle its lawsuit, without admitting wrongdoing.
facts.quote: Merrill Lynch was the county's chief investment banker at the time...and now has agreed to pay the county 400 million dollars.

facts.claim: In August 1998 Merrill Lynch settled a separate SEC administrative proceeding arising from the Orange County matter and agreed to a $2 million civil penalty.
facts.quote: In August 1998, Merrill Lynch settled an administrative proceeding and agreed to a $2 million civil penalty.

facts.claim: At a California Senate committee hearing in January 1995 Citron said that Merrill Lynch salesman Michael Stamenson had repeatedly encouraged the county to borrow money and buy volatile derivative securities; Merrill Lynch denied that it advised the county or devised its strategy.
facts.quote: Citron said Merrill salesman Michael Stamenson "repeatedly encouraged" the county to borrow money and to buy volatile derivative securities.

sources.title: Citron Says Merrill Lynch 'Guided' Risky Investments

connections.claim: Michael Stamenson, a broker in Merrill Lynch's San Francisco office, sold most of the government-agency notes that Orange County bought from Merrill Lynch under Citron; before a state Senate committee he said he had tried to warn Citron as early as 1992 and that Citron, not Merrill Lynch, controlled the portfolio.
connections.quote: sold mainly by Stamenson, 54, a star broker in Merrill's San Francisco branch office

openQuestions: The site's figures for leverage (a roughly $7.4 billion pool levered to about $20 billion) and losses (about $1.64 billion) were not confirmed from the sources returned; the Jorion case study is the likely source and should be read in full.

The site gives the Merrill settlement as $400 million; one source returned gives $437 million (June 1998). NPR's contemporaneous report says $400 million; the difference may reflect related payments and should be checked.

How the one-year jail sentence was served (work furlough) and whether a suspended six-year term was also imposed appears only in secondary sources (Patch, an AI-generated encyclopedia); confirm from the sentencing record.

The 'Merrill Lynch sued by the SEC' connection in the Raabe entry is Citron being sued alongside Raabe, not Raabe suing Citron; the relation 'sued by' is used for the SEC action and the owner may prefer 'other'.
The entity id michael-stamenson is typed 'unknown' in entities.json; he is a person.
